newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn experts see tensions if France weakens on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bonn experts see tensions if France weakens on EMU.

text.p: Germany opposes further weakening of Europe's monetary union (EMU) and any bid to do so by a French Socialist government could raise serious tensions with Paris, Bonn foreign policy strategists said on Tuesday.

Commenting on Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decision to step down, they said the possibility that opposition leader Lionel Jospin could win next Sunday's second round of parliamentary elections was causing concern in pro-European Bonn.

Deputies and foreign policy experts from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) told Reuters they assumed Jospin did not want to delay the planned 1999 launch of the single currency, a key element in years of Franco-German joint efforts for further European integration.
But if he wins on Sunday, he will be under heavy pressure to fulfil promises to scrap an austerity drive meant to meet the EMU criteria and include Italy among the first EMU members.
Bonn fears this would lead to an unstable and weak currency that might not live up to the strict conditions set for it.
"We must interpret the criteria strictly," one CDU member of parliament insisted. "We have some leeway, but not much."
A CDU strategist said Italy was for German voters so synonymous with fast-and-loose budgetting that Bonn could not convince them EMU was stable if Rome were in from the start.
"The prejudice here against Italy is gigantic," he said. "It would be very difficult to have parliament accept a wider circle of participants including Italy.
"If France tried to impose that, it would lead to a lot more tension than we already have on monetary union."

Another policy specialist said: "If a Socialist government is elected, there is a danger Jospin would take measures that would disqualify France for EMU. This is the uncertainty we will have until Sunday, and maybe even after that."
Helmut Haussmann, European affairs spokesman for Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners, said he was concerned about Jospin being dependent on the eurosceptical Communists.

Even if the centre-right majority was returned, it might pick as prime minister the outgoing parliamentary speaker Philippe Seguin, leader of the anti-Maastricht camp in France's 1992 referendum which almost scuttled the whole unity drive.
"If Seguin got in, the scepticism (here) would rise," Haussmann told German Radio. He added, though, that he did not expect France's European policy to change fundamentally.
Several experts also thought that Jospin, if elected, would soon have to move into line with President Jacques Chirac's European policy, which is much closer to Chancellor Kohl's.

But they expressed concern that volatile French voters, having succeeded in chasing Juppe from office, could push Jospin to spend more than Paris can if it wants to meet the three percent budget deficit target for EMU.
One said a Socialist victory on Sunday could put pressure on Chirac as well, forcing him to ease his austerity programme and try to live up to the promises of his 1995 campaign.
Jospin would risk plummeting to Juppe's record low levels of popularity if he won election on a mildly Eurosceptical platform and then turned around to support austerity, he said.
Another strategist said he would call his contacts in Paris to ask if under French law the president can overrule a prime minister who wants to borrow more to pay for social programmes.

One probable reaction to a Jospin victory would be a round of consultations between Germany and the Benelux countries -- the other presumed members of an EMU "hard core" -- to agree which French policy options they would or would not support.

Several experts voiced concern that an anti-European mood could grow in France over the summer, as it did in 1992, if the new government does not make clear decisions and statements on EMU soon after taking office.

Any weakening of France's will to launch EMU on time and within the strict confines of the Maastricht treaty could encourage Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to argue for a softer line on the monetary union too, one expert said.

"A lot will depend on the SPD here because Kohl is determined not to have EMU voted in with only a narrow majority," he said. The German parliament must approve the decision to join the third phase of monetary union.
"They could say the French have stopped their austerity drive so we can too," he said. "Or they could say the French have made EMU so weak that it is not stable enough to start."
